abstract: Autophagosome formation requires cells to mobilize lipids for phagophore expansion and completion while maintaining lipid homeostasis during nutrient stress. How lipid intermediates are partitioned between membrane synthesis and neutral lipid storage under these conditions remains unclear. Here, we identify ER-vacuole tether Mdm1 as a regulator of starvation-induced autophagy in budding yeast. Loss of Mdm1 reduced autophagic flux despite preserved TORC1 responses to starvation and impaired autophagosome completion, as indicated by the accumulation of perivacuolar Atg8-positive structures and reduced protease protection. Lipidomic analyses revealed decreased phosphatidylinositol (PI) in whole cells and Atg8-enriched membrane fractions, accompanied by increased diacylglycerol (DAG) and storage lipids. Derepression of phospholipid synthesis through OPI1 deletion or inhibition of triacylglycerol synthesis restored autophagic flux. Remarkably, exogenous DAG also rescued autophagy despite elevated endogenous DAG in Mdm1-deficient cells. DAG supplementation increased PI abundance and improved protease protection, linking changes in lipid metabolism to autophagosome completion. Together, these findings implicate Mdm1 in coordinating membrane phospholipid homeostasis with neutral lipid metabolism and suggest that the metabolic availability of lipid intermediates contributes to efficient autophagosome formation during starvation.
